newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr at rest, builds rate immunity.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr at rest, builds rate immunity.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished a shade firmer Friday but was hardly changed on the week and showed no sign of breaking its month-old US$0.7855/7965 range.

Today's steady performance was stronger than it seemed, however, since most traders had expected the currency to crumble in the face of frantic rate cut speculation following weak domestic employment figures on Thursday.

"The AUD should have kicked lower offshore, but it didn't," said one. "The market was as skittish as it could be about a cut this morning but we still had plenty of bids in the US$0.7860/70 area. It's hard to say, but I think an easing is in the price."

By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar was making itself at home at US$0.7890/95 from an early US$0.7895/00 and US$0.7870/75 late here Thursday. It finished last week at US$0.7896/01 and in between was confined in a US$0.7855/7925 range.
Support looked solid at US$0.7870 after defeating all attempts to break lower following Thursday's weak employment data, while resistance was evident at US$0.7900 and US$0.7925.

On the crosses it overcame an early wobble to push to 87.85/95 yen from a 87.47 low and 87.52/62 late Thursday. Again, it was not a hundred miles from last Friday's 88.02/12 finish, reflecting the growing range mentality of the market.
In trade weighted terms the unit inched to 58.4 from a 58.2 finish Thursday, but was unchanged from last Friday's close.
Traders had expected the currency to break lower offshore after Thursday's steep 34,100 fall in September employment brought rate cut speculation to fever pitch.

Exporter and options-related buying held the line at US$0.7870 and saw the currency open near 79 cents, but selling resumed ahead of the Reserve Bank's morning market operation, where it would normally signal a change in policy.
In the event the bank kept its silence and bears had to cover their short positions.
The currency then hit a pocket of turbulence when US$/yen slid below 111.00, but again steadied as Japanese buying helped the U.S. unit rally to end at 111.34/39.

Traders said investors seemed to have come to terms with the likelihood of domestic rates being cut by 0.5 point to 6.50 percent before year end, and such an easing would not now be the bearish disaster many had feared a few weeks ago.

The futures market, however, was toying with the idea of a couple of cuts and had taken the March 90-day bill contract to an implied 6.36 percent in anticipation. If that view gained credence, the dollar would come under greater pressure.
The risk of a U.S. rate rise reared its ugly head overnight after weekly jobless claims data showed a steep 22,000 fall to 319,000 when analysts had looked for 342,000.
The data sparked talk October payrolls would more than make up for September's surprise drop and put a tightening back on the Federal Reserve's agenda.

On the domestic front analysts were hoping the RBA's october bulletin, which includes the bank's assessment of the economy in the September quarter, next week would shed some light on the outlook for monetary policy. The bank used its Q2 bulletin to drop the first hint that an easing was being considered.
The RBA has so far been upbeat on the outlook for the economy in 1997 and the chief danger to the currency was if it scaled back its expectations there.
That would be taken by the bond market as an admission more than one easing might be needed to get the economy moving again.
The worse case scenario could see the dollar test the pivotal uS$0.7810 chart level, a break of which would open the way for a return to August's US$0.7680 low.
On the topside, the currency needed to clear and close above US$0.7965 to restore confidence in its long term uptrend to US$0.8340. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
